inline.s: Far removed from the Sage: it has been a very long time since the Buddha was alive in the world.
Wrong wrought within the heart, calamity falls on the frame; no need to cry of grievance nor put the blame on another.
If you would not incur the karmic offenses of the unceasing hell, never slander the Tathagata's wheel of the true Dharma.

Wrong is wrought within the heart, and the calamitous retribution falls upon the body; this is all one's own doing and receiving, so there is no need to cry of grievance, and still less to blame another. If you would not incur the evil karma of the unceasing hell, then never slander the Tathagata's wheel of the true Dharma.
Lay the blame: to blame it on another.
In the woods of sandalwood stand no mingled trees; deep and dense and dark the lion takes his ease.
In the quiet forest he roams alone; far away the birds and beasts are flown.
The sandalwood forest has no mixed trees; deep, dense, and secluded the lion dwells there. In the tranquil forest he wanders alone, while birds and beasts all flee far away.
Sandal (
zhan
): that is, sandalwood. Lush and deep: the forest is thick and deep; the character here is the same as the one meaning "sinking", as "deep".
The lion cub, with all the throng behind, at three years old can roar a mighty sound.
If a wild beast pursues the Dharma king in strife, a hundred-year-old goblin chatters at life.

The lion cub has all the beasts following behind; by three years of age it can give a great roar. Those veteran purveyors of false beliefs (the wild jackals) contend against the Buddha's true Dharma, like a hundred-year-old goblin vainly opening its mouth to howl.

The lion cub: a metaphor for the advancing bodhisattva of sharp faculties, with the many following behind him. At three years old can give a great roar: the advancing bodhisattva of sharp faculties, having cultivated for no great length of time, can already expound the most supreme Mahayana (the great roar). Wild jackal (
han

): the meanest of all wild beasts. The wild jackal pursuing the Dharma king: a metaphor for those who preach error contending against the Buddha's true Dharma. "Pursuing" here means contending; for example, one says "contending for power". A hundred-year-old goblin vainly opening its mouth: "vainly" means to no purpose.
The perfect and sudden teaching
knows no
favoritism; if a doubt will not be settled, at once one must contend.
It is not that this mountain monk parades himself and others; it is lest in your practice you fall into the pit of annihilation and of eternalism.

The perfect and sudden teaching does not indulge human feeling; if there is a doubt unsettled, then one must debate it until it is clear. It is not that I would assert myself to win a personal contest of losing or winning; it is only for fear that in your practice you may fall into the trap of the view of annihilation and the view of eternalism.

The two views of annihilation and eternalism: the view of annihilation and the view of eternalism. The view of annihilation is the heterodox view insisting that after death the body and mind are cut off and there is no further rebirth; the view of eternalism is the heterodox view insisting that body and mind are permanent and never extinguished.
Not-not is not, and is is not the is; an error of a hair's breadth takes you a thousand miles astray.
If right, the Dragon Girl at once becomes a Buddha; if wrong, the Good Star falls while still in life.

Not is not, and is is; an error of a hair's breadth is a loss of a thousand miles. If correct, then the Dragon Girl at once becomes a Buddha; if wrong, then Good Star falls headlong into the unceasing hell in this very body.

An error of a hair's breadth, a loss of a thousand miles: though at the outset the deviation is ever so slight, the outcome as it develops is a vast error. The Dragon Girl's becoming a Buddha: the eight-year-old Dragon Girl, through the merit of upholding the Lotus Sutra, becomes a Buddha in that very body. Good Star: the son born to Shakyamuni Buddha while he was still the crown prince. After he left home, he cut off the afflictions of the realm of desire and attained the fourth dhyana. But later, by associating with evil companions, he lost the liberation he had gained, and then held that there was no Dharma of nirvana, gave rise to the heterodox view denying cause and effect, and even conceived an evil mind toward the Buddha, so that in that very life he fell into the unceasing hell.
In my early years I piled up learning, and also sought out commentaries and searched the sutras and treatises.
Distinguishing names and marks I knew no rest, like counting sand at the sea's bottom, laboring only to trap myself.

In my youth I heaped up learning, and also explored commentaries and pored over the sutras and treatises. Without rest, I applied myself to sorting out the names and marks (seeking only understanding, not rising from understanding into practice
, from practice attaining realization
), just as
one who reaches the bottom of the sea and, instead of taking the treasure, counts the grains of sand
, only to trap oneself in vain.

Master Shenhui is telling of how in his early years he too took a roundabout road. Had he not repented in time, he too would have erred by a hair's breadth and lost a thousand miles, and squandered a whole lifetime.

Names and marks: the terms and phrases of Buddhism. Counting sand at the sea's bottom: reaching the bottom of the sea and, instead of taking the treasure, counting the grains of sand. This is to say that in exploring the commentaries and studying the sutras and treatises, one should use the finger pointing at the moon and see the moon by following the finger (rising from understanding into practice, and through practice attaining realization). If one puts all one's energy into sorting out and studying names and marks, that is taking the finger that points at the moon as the moon itself and working on it, and so one falls onto a wrong path. The ancient worthy warns: one should use the finger to see the moon, and must not take the finger for the moon.

Yet I was sternly rebuked by the Tathagata: what benefit is there in counting another's treasures? Ever stumbling on the path of awakening, I sought in vain; for many years I toiled as a guest in the dust.

Again and again I was severely reproved by the Buddha; of what benefit to oneself is counting another's treasures (from morn to night counting another's treasures, yet having not half a coin of one's own)? Ever stumbling along the path of awakening (the bodhi way) and walking in vain, for many years I needlessly traveled about in the wind and dust, going from one teacher to another.
What benefit is there in counting another's treasures: the sutras, treatises, and commentaries are all guides for practice. If one does not apply them to one's own practice and put them into action,
then one is "counting another's treasures from morn to night, yet having not half a coin of one's own"; what benefit is that to oneself?
Stumbling (
ceng
): to be beset by hardships.
With a skewed nature, one misreads understanding, and fails to reach the Tathagata's perfect and sudden design.
The two vehicles are diligent but lack the mind of the Way; the heterodox are clever but have no wisdom.

With skewed faculties and mistaken understanding, one cannot comprehend the Tathagata's perfect and sudden Dharma-door. Though the two vehicles are diligent, they lack the mind of bodhi; though the heterodox are clever, they lack the wisdom of liberation.
Nature and faculties: the various natures and faculties. Bodhi: the wisdom that cuts off all afflictions and ignorance and realizes nirvana.

Also foolish, also dull and doting, upon an empty fist they build a real understanding; taking the finger for the moon, they labor in vain, and in the sphere of roots and objects forge all manner of fancies.

Foolish too, and dull and silly, they take real understanding to be born upon an empty fist (the expedient sayings), and, falsely clinging to the finger pointing at the moon as the bright moon, waste their effort; in the sphere of the roots, the dusts, and the dharmas (the five aggregates, the twelve sense-fields, and the eighteen elements) they vainly fancy and conjecture.
Dotting (
ai
): foolish, without knowledge.
Empty fist: to make a fist of an empty hand to startle children; a metaphor for the expedient sayings used to skillfully subdue sentient beings. The Ratnakuta Sutra says:

"As with an empty fist one lures a child, showing it a promise of something to make it glad, then opening the hand and finding nothing, the child thereupon wails again. So too the Buddhas, inconceivable, skillfully subdue the sort of sentient beings, knowing that the nature of things has no existence, and by provisional names set up and display them in the world."
The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says:
"When I sat at the place of enlightenment, wisdom was not to be had. With an empty fist one beguiles children, so as to save them all."

The finger pointing at the moon: the finger that points out the moon. The finger pointing at the moon is the finger that indicates the moon. Buddhism likens "true thusness" to the "moon", so for those who do not know true thusness (the moon), it uses various dharmas (the finger pointing at the moon) to explain true thusness (the moon). The finger pointing at the moon is a metaphor for the various dharmas spoken by the Buddha, that is, the eighty-four thousand Dharma-doors and the more than five thousand fascicles of scriptures. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
The sutra teachings
(all the scriptural teachings)
, are like the finger pointing at the moon. If one then sees the moon, one knows that what was pointed at was after all not the moon
(one then knows that the finger is after all not the moon)

Sutra: translated into Chinese as "connecting scripture", the general name for all the Buddha-dharma. "Connecting" is to connect above with the wonderful principle of all Buddhas and connect below with the faculties of sentient beings. "Scripture" means warp-threads, stringing the meaning together so that it is not scattered; it also means canonical text. Roots, objects, and dharmas: the five aggregates, twelve sense-fields, and eighteen elements. Five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Twelve sense-fields: the six external objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects) and the six internal faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). Eighteen elements: the six objects, six faculties, and six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness).
Not seeing a single dharma, that is the Tathagata; only then may one be called the Lord of Contemplation.
Awakened, the obstructions of karma are originally empty; not yet awakened, one must repay the debt from a former life.

Seeing no dharma as real, one is the Tathagata; only then is one called the Lord of Contemplation (Avalokiteshvara). Realizing the unborn dharmas, the obstructions of karma are originally empty; while one has not yet realized, one must still repay the debts of a former life.
Not seeing a single dharma, that is the Tathagata: "not seeing a single dharma" means not taking any single dharma as real and clinging to its mark. The Diamond Sutra says:
"All marks are false and vain."
It also says:
"To be free of all marks is to be called all the Buddhas."
The Three-Part Service of Zhongfeng says:
"The Buddhas, within the manifest arising and ceasing, see only the unborn; sentient beings, within the serene and unborn, see only arising and ceasing."
Lord of Contemplation:
in the realm where things and principle are unobstructed, one contemplates and reaches freedom. The Sixth Patriarch says:
"Originally not a single thing; where could dust alight?"
(The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch). Debt (
su
): the karmic debt of a former lifetime.

Hungry, one meets the royal banquet and cannot eat; sick, one meets the king of physicians and how shall one be cured? Practicing meditation within the realm of desire is the power of the unborn view; the lotus born in fire at last is not destroyed.
The brave giver, having transgressed, awakens to the unborn, and of old became a Buddha, and is here now.]

Hungry, yet meeting the royal feast and not eating, how can one be filled? Sick, yet meeting the king of physicians and not taking the medicine, how can one be healed? Practicing meditation within the sphere of desire is due to the power of the unborn view, like the red lotus that springs up in fire and is never harmed. The Bhikshu Yongshi (Brave Giver), though he had violated the two grave precepts of lust and killing, because he realized the patience of the unborn, long ago became a Buddha, named the Tathagata Precious Moon, and is here still.
Cured (
chai
): healed of illness.
The brave giver, having transgressed, awakens to the unborn, and of old became a Buddha, and is here now:
(The Bhikshu Yongshi had a secret affair with a woman and poisoned her husband,)

and his mind was filled with great remorse: "I have practiced the dharma of lust and also taken a human life. Alas! How strange! I am now a denizen of hell." At that time there was a bodhisattva named Nasikun
ju

tara, who said to Yongshi: "Bhikshu, do not fear; I now have the power to give you fearlessness." He thereupon entered the samadhi of the precious seal, and from his body produced innumerable Buddhas, who all in one voice spoke this verse: "All dharmas are like images in a mirror, and also like the moon in water; ordinary beings, with deluded minds, discriminate between folly, hatred, and love." The Bhikshu Yongshi, seeing the miraculous transformations of these transformation-Buddhas, reflected and chose among all dharmas, left all the covers and entanglements, and realized the patience of the unborn. Now he has become a Buddha, in the west, at a distance measured by the sands of the Ganges from this buddha-land; there is a land named Constant Light, and the Buddha is named the Tathagata Precious Moon."
(The Sutra of Purifying Karmic Obstructions)

Covers and entanglements: the five covers and ten entanglements. Five covers: five kinds of afflictions. "Cover" is another name for affliction, because afflictions cover over people's mind-nature so that wholesome dharmas do not arise. The five covers are: greed, anger, sloth-and-sleep, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt. Restlessness-and-remorse: restlessness and remorse; both of these states make the mind unable to be at peace and give rise to affliction. Restlessness: the waves of thought that cannot be gathered in. Ten entanglements: ten kinds of afflictions. "Entanglement" is another name for affliction, because afflictions tie up the body and mind of sentient beings so that they cannot escape birth and death or realize nirvana. The ten entanglements are: shamelessness, lack of self-respect, jealousy, stinginess, remorse, sloth-and-sleep, restlessness, sluggishness, anger, and concealment (hiding one's own wrongdoing).
The lion's roar, the fearless teaching, I deeply sigh for the muddled and stubborn who only know that grave offenses obstruct bodhi, and see not the secret instruction opened by the Tathagata.
The lion's roar, the fearless teaching; I deeply lament (
jie
) those muddled fellows who only know that grave offenses obstruct bodhi, and yet do not see the secret of liberation revealed by the Tathagata.

The lion's roar: the Buddha's preaching of the Dharma sounds through the ten directions, and all the hosts of Mara are subdued, just as when a lion roars all the hundred beasts are cowed. Fearless teaching: the Buddha speaks in the midst of the assembly, calm and without fear. Muddled (
meng
): confused. Stubborn (
da
): a description of those who, thick and hard like cowhide, are stubborn and do not understand principle.
Two bhikshus violated lust and killing; Upali's firefly-light added to their guilt; the great Vimalakirti at once dissolved their doubt, like the blazing sun melting the frost and snow.

There were two bhikshus who violated the two grave precepts of lust and killing; the admonition of the Venerable Upali, like the firefly's light, only increased the burden of their guilt; the great Vimalakirti taught them repentance through real marks and at once dispelled their doubt, just as the red sun dissolves the frost and snow.

Two bhikshus violated lust and killing, Upali's firefly-light added to their guilt, the great Vimalakirti at once dissolved their doubt: There were two bhikshus dwelling in the mountains, in a small hut, cultivating. One bhikshu went out, and the other fell asleep. A wood-gathering woman, taking advantage of the sleeping bhikshu, secretly committed lust with him. When the bhikshu woke he was filled with great remorse. The bhikshu who had gone out returned to the hut and was told of this. Hearing it, he flew into a rage and went in search of the woman to teach her a lesson. The woman was frightened and fled, and in her panic stumbled and fell into a deep pit and died. These two bhikshus, deeply feeling their offense, went together to the Venerable Upali to seek repentance. The Venerable's admonition only made them the more distressed. The great Vimalakirti, learning of it, upbraided the Venerable Upali, saying: "You should not disturb their minds and increase their offense; rather you should teach them how to put it away. You must know that the nature of offense is not within, not without, and not in between. Where there is a defiled mind there are defiled sentient beings; where there is a pure mind there are pure sentient beings. Where there is delusion there is defilement on the mind; where there is no delusion the mind is pure. All dharmas are false views, empty and unreal, born from delusion. Offense arises from the mind; one should repent it from the mind; when the defilement of the mind is extinguished, the offense too is extinguished." The two bhikshus, hearing this, at once had their doubt and remorse dispelled, and awakened to the unsurpassed mind of the Way. (See the Vimalakirti Nirdeśa Sutra
Chapter on the Disciples, third.)
Offense arises from the mind, and one should repent it with the mind; when the mind is gone the offense too is gone; both mind and offense gone, both empty — this is called true repentance."
The Vimalakirti Nirdeśa Sutra says:
"Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure."
The Sutra of Contemplating Bodhisattva Samantabhadra says:
"All the oceans of karmic obstruction arise from delusion. If one would repent, sit upright and contemplate the real mark. All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can melt them away."
(See the notes in detail in
Eliminating Old Karma
The Sutra on the Mind-Contemplation of the Great Vehicle says:
"If one can repent in accord with the Dharma, all afflictions are entirely removed; as a conflagration at the end of an age destroys the world, burning up Mount Sumeru and the great seas."
Inconceivable, the power of liberation, whose wondrous functions are numberless as the sands of the Ganges and without limit.

How dare I begrudge the toil of the four offerings; even ten thousand taels of gold can be received. Broken body and crushed bones are not enough to repay, but one line understood at once surpasses a hundred billion.

Inconceivable, the power of liberation through the unborn; its many wondrous functions, as countless as the sands of the Ganges, have no limit. How dare I decline the toil of making the four offerings; even ten thousand taels of gold can be borne with ease. To smash the body and crush the bones would not be enough to repay the Buddha's great kindness; a single line clearly understood at once leaps beyond hundreds of billions of eons of gradual progression.

The four offerings: to make offerings with the four kinds of requisites: food, clothing, bedding, and medicine. Even ten thousand taels of gold can be received: even the offering of ten thousand taels of gold can be borne with ease. The Essential Instructions on Cultivating the Mind says:

"If one awakens to this mind, truly it is what is called treading no ladder but directly mounting the ground of Buddhahood, transcending the three realms at every step, and returning home, at once severing all doubt. One then becomes the teacher of gods and humans, with compassion and wisdom mutually supporting, fulfilled in the twofold benefit, and worthy of the offerings of gods and humans, daily consuming ten thousand taels of gold. If you are thus, you are truly a great man, and the great work of a life is done."
(Translation:

If you awaken to this mind of empty stillness and numinous knowing, it is truly what is called treading no ladder but directly mounting the ground of Buddhahood, at every step transcending the three realms, and at once severing the doubt of whether one can return home (become a Buddha). You can then be the teacher of gods and humans, with compassion and wisdom mutually sustaining, fulfilled in the twofold benefit of self and others, able to receive the offerings of gods and humans, daily bearing the offering of ten thousand taels of gold. If you are like this, you are truly a great man, and the great work of a lifetime is done.

Mutually sustaining: to support one another. The twofold benefit: self-benefit and benefiting others. Seeking above the buddha-fruit is self-benefit; transforming sentient beings below is benefiting others. Daily consuming ten thousand taels of gold: this shows the vastness of merit and virtue. The old master of Guishan says:
"This old monk, once seated in meditation, can consume ten thousand taels of gold (
means he is worthy of bearing the offering of ten thousand taels of gold)
The ancient worthy says:
"If the venerable one has truly awakened, then turning the great earth into gold and churning the long river into buttermilk to offer the venerable one is not out of place
(to offer these to the venerable one is what is deserved)
. But if not, then for a single grain of rice or a single thread, one must drag the plow and haul the rake to repay it before one is done."
(From the Commentary on the Song of Enlightenment by the Virtuous Hongde)

One line understood at once surpasses a hundred billion: one line clearly understood at once leaps beyond hundreds of billions of eons of gradual progression. "One line" is the line in the Diamond Sutra:
"To be free of all marks is to be called all the Buddhas."
The king of dharmas, the highest and most supreme, to which the Tathagatas countless as the sands of the Ganges all together bear witness.
I now understand this wish-fulfilling jewel; those who believe and receive it all attain response.

The perfect and sudden Dharma-door is the king of dharmas, highest and most supreme; the Tathagatas countless as the sands of the Ganges all together bear witness to it. I now have penetrated this wish-fulfilling jewel (the perfect and sudden Dharma-door); those who believe and receive it will all be in accord.
[Clearly and distinctly see: not a single thing, no person either, and no Buddha. The thousand-great-thousand worlds are but a bubble on the sea; all sages and saints are like lightning in the sky.]

Clearly and distinctly one sees that there is no thing, no person, and also no Buddha. The countless worlds, as many as the sands of the Ganges, are like a bubble on the sea's surface; all sages and saints are like a flash of lightning in the empty sky.
Sands of worlds: worlds as many as the sands of the Ganges. Bubble (
ou
): a water bubble.
This passage is the realm of one who has realized the unborn dharmas. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

"Perfect enlightenment universally shines, quiescent and nondual, and within it the hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions of asamkhyeyas and inconceivable numbers of buddha-worlds, countless as the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky, rising and falling in confusion."

[The sun may be made cold, the moon may be made hot; the hosts of Mara cannot destroy this true teaching. The elephant's carriage climbs the towering peak with slow advance; who has ever seen a mantis able to stop its wheel

The sun may be made cold and the moon made hot, but the hosts of Mara cannot destroy the true teaching of the perfect and sudden. The elephant king's carriage advances slowly along the steep and towering peaks; who has ever seen a mantis able to block it?

The elephant's carriage: the carriage of the elephant king, a metaphor for the perfect and sudden Dharma-door. Towering peak: a high and steep peak, a metaphor for the dangerous turbid world. Wheel-tracks: the fixed route along which a carriage runs.

[The great elephant does not roam the rabbit's path; great awakening is not bound by petty details. Do not, with the view from a tube, slander the vast sky; if you are not yet enlightened, this is now my formula for you!]

The great elephant does not walk the small path of the rabbit; great awakening is not tied down by trifling details. Do not use your shallow opinion (the view from a tube) to slander the vast and profound sudden teaching. If you are not yet enlightened, then this Song of Enlightenment of mine is the secret formula guiding you!

The view from a tube: a shallow opinion, like looking at the sky through a tube, where the range seen is very small. Slandering the vast sky by the view from a tube: looking at the sky through a tube and saying the blue sky is only as wide as the tube's diameter. This is a metaphor for those who are not yet enlightened and vainly slander the sudden teaching with their own shallow opinions.
